data.title: Molly's milestone
data.description: Molly is an iconic girl character created by Hong Kong artist and designer Kenny Wong in 2006. She is recognised for her blonde hair, big green or blue eyes and signature pout. In 2016, Pop Mart discovered Molly and partnered with Wong to turn Molly into the company's first official Intellectual Property.

data.title: Newborn celebrated on social media for relaxed pose after delivery
data.description: A video of a baby's birth in Egypt has gone viral on social media, with viewers amazed at how remarkably relaxed he appeared as a doctor prepared to cut his umbilical cord shortly after delivery.

data.title: Competing ‘Nene Royal’ trademark bids emerge
data.description: Confusion has arisen over trademark applications for the stage name of Thai teen rocker Nene Royal, after a woman whose connection to the America’s Got Talent winner is unclear filed to register the name and logo — even before the artist’s managing company.

data.title: Cumbia comin' on strong
data.description: On the website of the Baltimore-based cumbia band Soroche is a big caps statement, "Cumbia Is The New Punk". This cumbia "fusion" outfit mixes cumbia, punk, ska, folk, a bit of rock'n'roll and anything else that takes their fancy into a heady Tropical concoction, or as the band puts it, "a danceable alchemy that crosses cultural dancefloors".

data.title: Lumphini’s lizards star in winning urban wildlife photo
data.description: A photograph of monitor lizards in Bangkok’s Lumphini Park by UK photographer Seth Forestson has won the Urban Wildlife category of Wildlife Photographer of the Year, an annual competition run by the Natural History Museum in London.

data.title: Thai films take the stage in Busan
data.description: The nerve centre of Asian cinema this week is in Busan, the South Korean port city and host of the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF). A premier film event on this side of the globe, the BIFF's role as a podium for outstanding Asian titles has long been cemented and this year Busan presents three new Thai films: Banjong Pisanthanakun's Inherit, a grand guignol adaptation of a classic horror novel; Phuttiphong Aroonpheng's The Burning Giants, in which a Karen man is trapped in a hazy fog of uncertainty; and Bua, an adolescent drama about a teenage girl in rural Thailand in the midst of the 1973 political unrest, directed by Inthira Charoenpura and Phensiri Klangsurin.
